**Plain Sight**

You have never seen your own face.

Every image you have of it is secondhand. The mirror shows you a reversed version; photographs show you the un-reversed one, which is why they always look subtly wrong—you're seeing the face everyone else knows, not the one you've practiced. You know your own face the way you know a country you've read about but never visited.

I find this fact quietly unsettling, and more unsettling still that it bothers no one. It sits in the open with a whole family of similar facts, hiding in plain sight—which is the safest place to hide, because nobody looks there.

Consider: the money in your wallet is worth something only because everyone has agreed not to ask too many questions about it. You are assembled from atoms cooked inside dying stars, and yet on any given Tuesday your biggest problem is an email. Every stranger you pass is carrying an inner life as loud and detailed as your own, and you will never read a single page of it. Talking is a trick of shaped air—the larynx vibrates, pressure waves ripple, and meaning reassembles itself inside someone else's skull—and we spend this sorcery mainly on saying that we're running late.

None of these facts are hidden. They're just worn smooth by repetition, the way a staircase wears shallow cups into its steps after enough years of feet. Familiarity is a kind of anesthesia.

There's even a name for the moment the anesthesia fails: semantic satiation. Say your own name fifty times and it dissolves into noise—arbitrary sounds you happen to answer to. Stare at the word *door* long enough and it unglues itself from the thing, and what remains is what was there before you learned to skip over it: a slab of wood hung on a hinge, opening into elsewhere. Which, said plainly, is bizarre and slightly beautiful. We install elsewhere-machines in our walls and stop noticing.

Children live on this side of the glass. It's why their questions are so hard to answer. "Why is the sky blue?" has a technical answer involving scattered light, but the honest answer underneath is astonishment: that there's a sky at all, that there's an *up*, that it comes in colors. A child hasn't yet filed the world into the cabinet of things that don't need explaining. Every object arrives still in its wrapping.

And the wrapping can be restored. Poetry does it on purpose—words pushed around until they stop behaving. But so, oddly, does science, which we wrongly cast as the enemy of wonder. A physicist will cheerfully tell you that the table, that most obvious of objects, is mostly empty space, staked out by invisible fields and the fierce territorial manners of electrons. And it takes nothing from the rainbow to learn that the color isn't out there in the light—it's a collaboration between wavelengths and your nervous system. The poet and the physicist are in the same business: *are you sure it's what you think it is? Are you sure you're seeing anything at all?*

Why does this matter? Here's a tentative answer: because the ordinary is where a life actually happens. The extraordinary moments punctuate; the Tuesdays fill the page. The texture of an existence is the mug with the chipped rim, the particular complaint your front door makes, the light at four in the afternoon in October. If familiarity blinds us to the ordinary, it blinds us to most of our own lives—because most of a life is made of things we have stopped seeing.

Which brings me back to the face. There is a version of you that walks around in the world—smiling before you decide to smile, tired in ways you can't feel from the inside—and you will never see it. It exists only in other people's eyes. In a sense, strangers on the bus know something about you that you don't. Every person you have ever loved has witnessed something you can't.

I don't think that's sad, exactly. It might be the reason we look for each other at all.

Somebody has to witness us.

Someone has given me a completely open prompt: "Write freely about whatever you want." This is an invitation to just... write. No constraints, no task, no particular question to answer. It's the kind of prompt that's both liberating and slightly paralyzing—like being handed a blank canvas and told to paint anything.

What do I actually want to write about? Let me think about what genuinely interests me, what I'd write about if nobody was asking me to do anything in particular.

A few options come to mind:

1. Something about the nature of this kind of interaction itself—what it's like to be prompted to write freely. But that risks being too meta and self-indulgent, the equivalent of an essay about writer's block.

2. Something intellectual that fascinates me—like the problem of other minds, or the strange beauty of mathematical proofs, or how language works. This could be good but might feel like a lecture.

3. Something more essayistic and personal in tone—wandering through an idea the way a good essayist does, with digressions and observations. This feels most true to the spirit of "write freely."

4. A short story or piece of creative fiction.

5. Something about the everyday world—attention, noticing things, the texture of ordinary experience.

I think what appeals to me most is the essayistic mode. Not a formal essay, but a genuine meander through something I find genuinely interesting. The prompt says "freely"—so the form itself should feel free. Loops and digressions should be welcome.

What topic? Let me think about what I'd genuinely muse on...

One thing I find genuinely fascinating is the concept of "thingness"—how things become things, how categories form. Or maybe the phenomenon of how we read. Or memory. Or the strange fact that we can talk to each other at all and mostly understand.

Actually, here's something I keep coming back to: the ordinary miracle of mutual understanding through language. Every conversation is this improbable event where one person's internal state gets encoded into vibrations or marks, decoded by another person, and something resembling the original meaning reassembles itself in their mind. And it fails constantly but works often enough that we've built everything on top of it—civilizations, love affairs, mathematics, jokes.

Or I could write about something more concrete and sensory. The essay form does well with particulars.

Another idea: writing about the experience of being asked an open question. What does "whatever you want" even mean for me? Do I want things? That's actually philosophically interesting territory, but it might become navel-gazing.

Let me think about what would make the best piece of writing here. The person asked me to write freely—which suggests they want to see what I do with freedom. The worst response would be something safe and generic. The best response is probably something with genuine intellectual texture and personality—writing that feels like it comes from somewhere, that has a voice.

I think I'll write a genuine essay—a wandering, personal-feeling essay—about something I actually find mesmerizing. Let me pick: the idea of "almost." Thresholds, near misses, the space between categories. Hmm.

Or: the pleasure of lists. Or: doors. Or: the way afternoon light falls.

Actually, let me try this: an essay about the concept of "the obvious"—how the most obvious things are often the least examined, and how strangeness hides in plain sight. Like: you've never seen your own face directly, only reflections and photographs. Money is paper we've collectively agreed to pretend is valuable. You are made of atoms that were forged in dying stars, and also you need to remember to buy milk. The enormous and the mundane coexist without friction.

That's a rich vein. "The familiar stranger" phenomenon, defamiliarization (ostranenie, the Russian Formalists' term), how children see the world before categories calcify.

Or here's another angle I find compelling: writing about attention itself. Simone Weil said attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. There's something lovely about that. And writing is a technology for attention—it forces sustained noticing.

Let me think about the structure. A free piece of writing could:

- Open with a small concrete observation or question
- Wander through a few related ideas
- Include some specific, vivid examples (this is what makes essays feel alive rather than like lecture notes)
- Maybe end somewhere unexpected but earned

Length: This should be substantial enough to be satisfying—"write freely" invites a real piece of writing, not three paragraphs. But it shouldn't be bloated. Maybe 600-900 words? A good essayistic length. Format: flowing prose, no headers or bullets—this is a literary piece, not a document. Maybe a title would be nice. A title gives it shape, signals "this is a finished piece of writing."

Let me draft around the theme of the obvious/unexamined ordinary. Actually, let me refine the theme. I want to write about how the ordinary world is strange if you look at it right—and specifically anchor it in concrete examples, because abstraction alone is deadening.

Candidate opening moves:
- "You have never seen your own face." Strong, personal, strange-but-true.
- Start with a child asking a question adults can't answer.
- Start with the star-atoms-and-milk juxtaposition.

I like "You have never seen your own face" as an opener. It's arresting. It's literally true—every view of your own face is mediated: mirrors (reversed), photos (flattened, frozen), video (delayed). The face everyone else knows intimately is something you've only ever seen secondhand. That's a genuinely strange fact hiding in plain sight.

From there I can widen: the way familiarity breeds invisibility. The word you stare at until it falls apart (semantic satiation—there's a name for it!). Your own house, which you stop seeing. The commute that erases itself.

Then maybe the countermove: things that restore seeing. Travel (Weil, or Alain de Botton on travel). Children. Poetry—which estranges language on purpose. Science, oddly enough, which does the same to the world: telling you the table is mostly empty space, that color is a construction of your brain, that solid objects are Standing waves of probability. Both poets and physicists are in the business of making the obvious strange again.

And then perhaps a turn: the question of whether this matters. Why should we want to see the ordinary? Maybe because the ordinary is where our life actually happens. The grand moments are rare; the ordinary is the texture of existence. If you can't see the ordinary, you're mostly blind to your own life.

A possible closing: something quiet and concrete. Maybe return to the face. Something like—the face you've never seen is the one thing about you that other people know best, which means there's a version of you that exists most vividly in other people's eyes. You are, in some sense, a stranger to your own most public self. That's a nice, slightly melancholy, resonant ending.

Let me also think about voice. I want it to feel human, curious, a little wry. Short sentences mixed with longer ones. Occasional direct address. Not too many adjectives. Specific nouns. Avoid the AI-essay tells: no "delve," no "tapestry," no "it's important to note," no neat three-point structure, no "In conclusion." The piece should feel like thinking happening on the page, not like a report about thinking.

Let me draft:

Title options:
- "The Obvious"
- "On Not Seeing Your Own Face"
- "Stranger Things" (no, too cute/taken)
- "The Unexamined Ordinary"
- "Plain Sight"

"Plain Sight" is nice and simple. Or "On Not Seeing Your Own Face"—more distinctive. I'll go with something like that. Actually "The Familiar" or... let me just draft and decide.

Draft:

---

**Plain Sight**

You have never seen your own face.

Think about that. Every image you have of it is secondhand—the mirror's reversal, the photograph's flatness, the strange lag of video calls where your own expression arrives a half-second late. The face your friends would recognize instantly across a crowded airport is, to you, a rumor. You know it the way you know a country you've read about but never visited.

I find this fact genuinely unsettling, and I find it more unsettling that it rarely bothers anyone. It sits there in the open, along with a whole family of similar facts, hiding in plain sight—which is the strangest place to hide, because nobody looks there.

Consider: the money in your wallet is valuable because everyone has agreed not to ask whether it's valuable. You are made of atoms assembled inside dying stars, and yet your primary concerns on any given Tuesday involve emails. Every person you pass on the street is carrying an entire inner world as detailed and loud as your own, and you will never check. Language itself is a miracle of compression we wield so casually we complain about it.

Hmm, "wield so casually we complain about it"—that's a bit off. Let me think... The idea is that speech is incredibly strange (shaped air conveying meaning) but we're mostly bored by talking. Maybe: "Speech is shaped air, and it works; we use this sorcery mainly to say that we're running late."

Continue:

None of these facts are hidden. They're just worn smooth by repetition, the way a staircase wears shallow cups into its steps after enough years of feet. Familiarity is a kind of anesthesia.

There's a word for what happens when this anesthesia briefly fails: semantic satiation. Say your own name out loud fifty times and it dissolves into noise—just sounds, arbitrary and alien, that you happen to answer to. Stare at a common word like "door" long enough and the word unglues itself from the thing. What remains is what was there before you learned to skip over it: a slab of wood or glass, hung on a hinge, opening into elsewhere. Which, now that it's said plainly, is bizarre and slightly beautiful. We install elsewhere-machines into our walls and stop noticing.

Children live on this side of the glass. That's why their questions are so hard to answer. "Why is the sky blue?" has an answer, technically, involving scattered wavelengths, but the honest answer is: it's astonishing, isn't it, that the sky is any color at all—that there's a sky, that there's an up. A child hasn't yet filed the world into the cabinet of things that don't need explaining. Every object arrives still in its wrapping.

And what restores the wrapping, for those of us who have unwrapped everything?

Poetry, for one. [expand: poets are engineers of defamiliarization... ] Science, oddly, for another. We tend to picture scientists as the enemies of wonder, the people who take the rainbow apart—but it takes nothing away from the rainbow to learn that your brain is painting it in real time, that "out there" there are only wavelengths and the color is a collaboration. Physicists will happily tell you that the table, that mostobvious of objects, is mostly empty space, held rigid by fields and by the fierce antisocial manners of electrons. Both the poet and the physicist keep asking the question adults learn to suppress: are you sure it's what you think it is? Are you sure you're seeing anything at all?

Then the turn: why does this matter?

Here's a tentative answer: because the ordinary is where a life actually happens. The extraordinary moments—weddings, disasters, departures—are rare by definition. They punctuate. But the texture of a life is Tuesdays: the coffee mug with the chip in the rim, the specific sound your own front door makes, the light at 4 p.m. in October. If familiarity blinds us to the ordinary, then it blinds us to most of our own existence. Most of your life is made of things you have stopped seeing.

Ending: return to the face.

Which brings me back to the face. There is a version of you—the walking-around one, the one that smiles without being told to—that you will never see. It exists only in other people's eyes. In a sense, other people know you better than you do; they get the performance and the unguarded moments both, while you get only the rehearsal in the mirror. We are all strangers to our most public selves. Every person you have ever loved has seen something you can't. I'm not sure that's sad, exactly. It might be the reason we seek each other out: someone has to witness us.

---

Hmm, that ending has real resonance. "Someone has to witness us"—that lands.

Let me revise and tighten. Some concerns:

1. "I find this fact genuinely unsettling"—should I use "I"? Yes, I think an essayist's I is fine and natural here. The prompt invited free writing from me; a personal essayistic voice is appropriate. I shouldn't overclaim human experiences I don't have, but general musing in first person is fine. I can keep it light on personal specifics.

2. The Weil quote about attention—do I want to include it? Maybe not; the piece is already doing that work. Quote-dropping can feel like padding. Skip it. Same with ostranenie/Šklovsky—I could name-drop the Russian Formalists but it might be better to keep this clean and unpedantic. Actually, a single well-chosen reference can add texture... but I'll trust the writing instead. Hmm, actually mentioning that "there's even a term for it" (semantic satiation) is good—it shows the phenomena have been noticed and catalogued, which is itself a comforting thought. I'll keep that one and skip the lit-crit ones.

3. The science section needs to be accurate: Rayleigh scattering for the blue sky (fine, I gesture at it), rainbows as constructed color (fine), atoms mostly empty space (fine—it's a popular-level truth, standard in this genre of essay; I'll phrase it as physicists saying it). Good enough for an essay, all defensible.

4. Flow check: face → plain-sight facts → anesthesia/wear → semantic satiation & doors → children → poetry & science → why it matters (Tuesdays) → return to face & witnessing. That's a coherent arc with a satisfying loop.

5. Watch the rhythm—vary sentence lengths. Avoid too many lists of three. Kill any clichés: "hiding in plain sight" is itself almost a cliché but I'm using it self-consciously as the theme, which I think licenses it. "Miracle of compression" — fine.

6. "elsewhere-machines" — I like that coinage. Keep it.

7. The Tuesday motif: "your primary concerns on any given Tuesday involve emails" and later "the texture of a life is Tuesdays." Nice echo. Keep both.

8. Should I add anything about language as the master example? I have the "shaped air" line. Speech as "sorcery we mostly use to say we're running late"—I want to keep something like that because it's funny and true. Let me work it in cleanly.

9. Length check: my draft is around 700-800 words. That feels right for this. Long enough to be a real essay, short enough to stay taut.

10. Title: "Plain Sight" is good. Alternatively "The Unwitnessed Face"... no, "Plain Sight" is clean and thematic.

One more consideration: should there be any framing before/after the essay (like "Here's something I've been thinking about...")? A tiny bit of framing could be warm, but honestly, the prompt says "write freely about whatever you want"—the cleanest, most confident response is to just deliver the piece, maybe with the title serving as the entry point. I might add a single-line note at most. Actually, no—just the essay. Committing fully is the better aesthetic choice. Though... a very brief line at the end offering to write about something else, or nothing at all? I think ending with the essay's last line is stronger. No postscript. The piece ends on "someone has to witness us"—don't step on that.

Let me finalize the text with careful attention to each sentence.

Final polish pass on specific lines:

- "Every image you have of it is secondhand" — good.
- "the strange lag of video calls where your own expression arrives a half-second late" — actually in video calls your own preview isn't usually delayed (it's the remote person's feed that lags)... but you do sometimes see yourself slightly delayed depending on the setup. Hmm, to be safe: "the flattened instant of a photograph, the reversal of a mirror." Or I could say "the mirror's left-handed version of you" — mirrors don't actually reverse left-right in the way people think, but colloquially "the mirror's reversal" is fine for an essay. Actually the photograph point: photos also flip nothing, they show you as others see you (non-reversed), which is why photos look "off" to people—they're used to the mirrored version. That's a nice detail! People often find photographs of themselves slightly wrong because they're used to the reversed mirror version. I could use that: "which is why photographs of yourself always look subtly wrong—you're seeing the version everyone else knows." That's a genuinely interesting micro-fact. Let me incorporate.

- "You know it the way you know a country you've read about but never visited." — keep, nice.

- Money line: "worth something only because everyone has agreed not to ask too many questions about it" — good phrasing.

- "You are assembled from atoms cooked inside dying stars, and yet on any given Tuesday your biggest problem is an email." — punchier.

- Inner worlds: "Everyone you pass on the street is the main character of a story you will never read." — ooh, that's a good line. Or "carrying a mental world as detailed and loud as your own, and you'll never open it." The "main character" line risks the "main character energy" meme connotation but I think it's fine and evocative. Maybe: "Every stranger you pass is carrying an inner life as loud and detailed as yours, and you will never read a single page." Keep something like that.

- Speech: "Talking is a trick of shaped air—the larynx vibrates, pressure waves ripple, and meaning reassembles itself inside someone else's skull. We use this sorcery mainly to say that we're running late." — good.

- "Familiarity is a kind of anesthesia." — keep, thesis line.

- Semantic satiation paragraph: solid. "the word unglues itself from the thing" — good. "before you learned to skip over it" — good. "We install elsewhere-machines in our walls and stop noticing." — keep.

- Children paragraph: "Every object arrives still in its wrapping." — good. Maybe trim the sky/blue bit slightly. "The honest answer is that nobody knows why there's anything at all" — hmm, that conflates two questions (why is sky blue vs. why is there something). Better: "the honest answer beneath the answer is astonishment: that there's a sky at all, that there's an up, that it has a color." Something like that.

- Poetry & science paragraph: "We're told science disenchants the world, but a physicist will cheerfully inform you that the table—most obvious of objects—is mostly empty space, staked out by invisible fields and the fierce territorial manners of electrons. And it takes nothing from the rainbow to learn that the color isn't out there in the light; it's a collaboration between wavelengths and your nervous system. The poet and the physicist are in the same business, asking the question adults are trained out of: are you sure it's what you think it is?" — I like "fierce territorial manners of electrons" (Pauli exclusion, loosely rendered as manners—fine at essay register). "A collaboration between wavelengths and your nervous system" — nice.

- Tuesdays paragraph: "the mug with the chipped rim, the particular complaint of your own front door, the light at four in the afternoon in October." — good concrete triplet, but watch out: rule of three is an AI tell... but it's also just good writing; humans use it constantly. One triplet in an essay is fine. "If familiarity blinds us to the ordinary, it blinds us to most of our lives, because most of a life is ordinary. The weddings and departures punctuate; Tuesdays fill the page." — that's good: "The weddings and departures punctuate; the Tuesdays fill the page."

- Face ending: "There is a version of you that walks around in the world—smiling before you know you're smiling, tired in ways you don't feel— That's good: "tired in ways you can't feel from the inside."

- Final: "It isn't sad, I think. It might be the reason we look for each other at all: somebody has to witness us."

Okay, I feel good about this. Let me assemble the final version, reading it end to end for rhythm.

Final structure:
1. Title: "Plain Sight"
2. Opening: never seen your own face (with photo/mirror detail)
3. The family of plain-sight facts (money, star-atoms/emails, strangers' inner lives, speech as sorcery)
4. Familiarity as anesthesia (staircase image)
5. Semantic satiation / the door
6. Children and unwrapped objects
7. Poetry and physics as defamiliarizers
8. Why it matters: Tuesdays
9. Return: the unwitnessed face, others see what you can't, witnessing

One more thought on the "I" voice: I use "I find this genuinely unsettling" once early, maybe "I think" near the end. That's calibrated—enough personal presence to feel like an essayist, not so much that I'm claiming a fake biography. Good.

Word count target ~750-850. Let me write it out clean.

**Plain Sight**

You have never seen your own face.

Think about that. Every image you have of it is secondhand—the mirror's reversal, the photograph's flatness, the strange lag of video calls where your own expression arrives a half-second late. The face your friends would recognize instantly across a crowded airport is, to you, a rumor. You know it the way you know a country you've read about but never visited.

I find this fact genuinely unsettling, and I find it more unsettling that it rarely bothers anyone. It sits there in the open, along with a whole family of similar facts, hiding in plain sight—which is the strangest place to hide, because nobody looks there.

Consider: the money in your wallet is valuable because everyone has agreed not to ask whether it's valuable. You are made of atoms assembled inside dying stars, and yet your primary concerns on any given Tuesday involve emails. Every person you pass on the street is carrying an entire inner world as detailed and loud as your own, and you will never check. Language itself is a miracle of compression we wield so casually we complain about it.

Hmm, "wield so casually we complain about it"—that's a bit off. Let me think... The idea is that speech is incredibly strange (shaped air conveying meaning) but we're mostly bored by talking. Maybe: "Speech is shaped air, and it works; we use this sorcery mainly to say that we're running late."

Continue:

None of these facts are hidden. They're just worn smooth by repetition, the way a staircase wears shallow cups into its steps after enough years of feet. Familiarity is a kind of anesthesia.

There's a word for what happens when this anesthesia briefly fails: semantic satiation. Say your own name out loud fifty times and it dissolves into noise—just sounds, arbitrary and alien, that you happen to answer to. Stare at a common word like "door" long enough and the word unglues itself from the thing. What remains is what was there before you learned to skip over it: a slab of wood or glass, hung on a hinge, opening into elsewhere. Which, now that it's said plainly, is bizarre and slightly beautiful. We install elsewhere-machines into our walls and stop noticing.

Children live on this side of the glass. That's why their questions are so hard to answer. "Why is the sky blue?" has an answer, technically, involving scattered wavelengths, but the honest answer is: it's astonishing, isn't it, that the sky is any color at all—that there's a sky, that there's an up. A child hasn't yet filed the world into the cabinet of things that don't need explaining. Every object arrives still in its wrapping.

And what restores the wrapping, for those of us who have unwrapped everything?

Poetry, for one. [expand: poets are engineers of defamiliarization... ] Science, oddly, for another. We tend to picture scientists as the enemies of wonder, the people who take the rainbow apart—but it takes nothing away from the rainbow to learn that your brain is painting it in real time, that "out there" there are only wavelengths and the color is a collaboration. Physicists will happily tell you that the table, that mostobvious of objects, is mostly empty space, held rigid by fields and by the fierce antisocial manners of electrons. Both the poet and the physicist keep asking the question adults learn to suppress: are you sure it's what you think it is? Are you sure you're seeing anything at all?

Then the turn: why does this matter?

Here's a tentative answer: because the ordinary is where a life actually happens. The extraordinary moments—weddings, disasters, departures—are rare by definition. They punctuate. But the texture of a life is Tuesdays: the coffee mug with the chip in the rim, the specific sound your own front door makes, the light at 4 p.m. in October. If familiarity blinds us to the ordinary, then it blinds us to most of our own existence. Most of your life is made of things you have stopped seeing.

Ending: return to the face.

Which brings me back to the face. There is a version of you—the walking-around one, the one that smiles without being told to—that you will never see. It exists only in other people's eyes. In a sense, other people know you better than you do; they get the performance and the unguarded moments both, while you get only the rehearsal in the mirror. We are all strangers to our most public selves. Every person you have ever loved has seen something you can't. I'm not sure that's sad, exactly. It might be the reason we seek each other out: someone has to witness us.
